title: Evaluating Sources
sub: Visual and Written Evidence · Grades 5–8 · ELA · 30 minutes
objective: Students will evaluate the credibility of visual and written sources using the CRAAP test, identify indicators of bias, and distinguish between primary and secondary sources in order to become more discerning consumers of information.
materials: Spirit photography examples (1860s–1900s) — available online or in Mini Museum materials
Modern deepfake example or manipulated image (age-appropriate)
Two articles about the same event from different perspectives
CRAAP test poster or handout (included in student materials)
3–4 sources for practice evaluation (mix of reliable and unreliable)
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the Mini Museum:** The exhibition includes Victorian optical illusion cards and a stereoscope — both of which demonstrate how Victorians were fascinated by visual trickery. Spirit photography exploited this fascination AND people’s grief. The same principles apply today: manipulated images exploit our emotions and our trust in visual “evidence.”
**Option 2 — Virtual Visit:** Explore the exhibition online, or view individual artifacts at minimuseumproject.org/exhibitions/seeing-is-deceiving/artifacts

steps.title: The Ghost in the Photograph
script: Display a spirit photograph from the 1860s–1900s (William Mumler’s work is a good example).

“This photograph was taken in the 1860s. The photographer charged grieving families a lot of money because he claimed he could photograph the spirits of their dead loved ones. Look at it carefully. Do you think it’s real?”

screen.question: Look at it carefully. Do you think it’s real?

steps.purpose: Students judge a spirit photograph before they know how it was made.

steps.title: This is a fake
script: Let students share initial reactions. Then reveal: *“This is a fake. The photographer used a technique called double exposure to add ‘ghosts’ to his pictures. He made a fortune before being exposed as a fraud.”*

screen.question: The photographer used a technique called double exposure to add ‘ghosts’ to his pictures.

steps.purpose: The reveal: how the ghost got into the picture.

steps.title: How do we know what to believe?
script: “People have been manipulating images since photography was invented. Today we have Photoshop and AI deepfakes. The technology changes, but the challenge remains the same: How do we know what to believe? Today, you’re going to learn a systematic way to evaluate ANY source — visual or written — so you can protect yourself from being fooled.”

screen.question: The technology changes, but the challenge remains the same: How do we know what to believe?

steps.purpose: From one old fake to a method for judging any source today.
students: Today, you’re going to learn a systematic way to evaluate ANY source — visual or written.

steps.title: The CRAAP Test
script: *“Librarians and researchers use something called the CRAAP test to evaluate sources. Yes, it’s a funny name — but it helps you remember it!”*

cells: When was this created or updated?
Does this relate to your needs?

steps.purpose: The five letters at a glance, before taking each in turn.
students: Five questions to ask of any source.

steps.title: C · Currency
script: **C — Currency:** When was this created or updated?
Is the information recent enough for your topic?
Are links functional? Is the site maintained?
For images: When was the photo actually taken vs. when was it shared?

screen.question: Is the information recent enough for your topic? Are links functional? Is the site maintained? For images: When was the photo actually taken vs. when was it shared?

steps.purpose: Take one letter of the test at a time, with the questions to ask under it.
students: When was this created or updated?

steps.title: R · Relevance
script: **R — Relevance:** Does this relate to your needs?
Does it answer your question?
Who is the intended audience?
Is it at an appropriate level?

screen.question: Does it answer your question? Who is the intended audience? Is it at an appropriate level?

steps.purpose: Take one letter of the test at a time, with the questions to ask under it.
students: Does this relate to your needs?

steps.title: A · Authority
script: **A — Authority:** Who created this?
Who is the author/creator? What are their credentials?
Is there contact information?
What does the URL tell you? (.edu, .gov, .org, .com)

screen.question: Who is the author/creator? What are their credentials? Is there contact information? What does the URL tell you? (.edu, .gov, .org, .com)

steps.purpose: Take one letter of the test at a time, with the questions to ask under it.

steps.title: A · Accuracy
script: **A — Accuracy:** Is the information correct?
Can you verify this information elsewhere?
Are sources cited?
Are there spelling/grammar errors (often a red flag)?
For images: Has this been altered? Does reverse image search show different contexts?

screen.question: Can you verify this information elsewhere? Are sources cited? Are there spelling/grammar errors (often a red flag)? For images: Has this been altered? Does reverse image search show different contexts?

steps.purpose: Take one letter of the test at a time, with the questions to ask under it.

steps.title: P · Purpose
script: **P — Purpose:** Why does this exist?
Is it trying to inform, persuade, sell, or entertain?
Is it fact, opinion, or propaganda?
Does the author/creator have a bias or agenda?
For images: Was this created to document reality or to manipulate emotions?

steps.title: Practice Together
script: **Part 1: Practice Together (5 minutes)** — Display a clearly unreliable source (example: a satirical news site, an outdated webpage, or a heavily biased blog). Walk through the CRAAP test together:
*“Let’s check Currency first. When was this written?”*
*“Who’s the Authority here? Can we find information about the author?”*
*“What’s the Purpose? Is this trying to inform us or persuade us?”*

screen.question: Let’s check Currency first. When was this written? Who’s the Authority here? Can we find information about the author? What’s the Purpose? Is this trying to inform us or persuade us?

steps.purpose: Walk through the test together on a clearly unreliable source.
students: Walk through the CRAAP test together.

steps.title: Independent/Partner Practice
script: **Part 2: Independent/Partner Practice (7 minutes)** — Provide 2–3 sources for students to evaluate (mix of reliable and unreliable). Students can work individually or in pairs to apply the CRAAP test.
Suggested sources to include:
A Wikipedia article (discuss: useful starting point, but check the citations)
A news article from a reputable source
A clearly biased website or social media post
An image shared out of context (reverse image search reveals the truth)
steps.purpose: Students test a mix of reliable and unreliable sources on their own or in pairs.
students: Evaluate 2–3 sources: a mix of reliable and unreliable.

steps.title: Primary vs. Secondary Sources
script: “One more important distinction: Primary sources are original, firsthand accounts — a photograph taken at an event, a diary entry, an interview. Secondary sources analyze or interpret primary sources — a textbook chapter, a documentary, a news article about something.”

“Neither is automatically better, but knowing the difference matters. The spirit photographs we saw were PRIMARY sources — but they were still fake! Primary doesn’t mean true. You still need to apply the CRAAP test.”
steps.purpose: Primary or secondary, a source still needs the CRAAP test.
students: Primary sources are original, firsthand accounts.
Secondary sources analyze or interpret primary sources.
